title: US General Warns Pentagon He Cannot Defend Israel Without More Naval Forces
excerpt: The head of US European Command told the Pentagon that dwindling destroyer availability may force him to choose between defending American forces and protecting Israel.
body:
• Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, head of US European Command, warned the Pentagon he lacks sufficient naval forces to continue protecting Israel from Iranian ballistic missiles.
  • Without an additional destroyer, Grynkewich said he may be forced to prioritize US forces over Israeli defense, according to a Washington Post report.
  • US Patriot interceptor inventories have dropped from roughly 2,300 pre-war to fewer than 827, with THAAD stocks falling from 452 to under 278.
  • The warning comes as the Iran war strains US military resources and the Pentagon seeks $67 billion in emergency funding.

A top US general has warned his superiors that Washington lacks sufficient military power to continue defending Israel from Iranian missile attacks, according to a Washington Post report published Friday.

Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who leads US European Command, told the Pentagon that he does not have enough naval destroyers positioned in the eastern Mediterranean to maintain missile defense coverage for Israel. Unless Washington provides another destroyer, he will be forced to choose between defending US forces and protecting the ally, the report said.

Stockpile Crisis

The warning arrives as months of conflict with Iran have severely depleted America's arsenal of high-end missile defense interceptors. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that US Patriot interceptor inventories have fallen from roughly 2,300 before the war to fewer than 827. THAAD interceptor stocks have dropped from 452 to under 278.

https://x.com/mayegun1805/status/2083631214288634108

"If you look at what we've expended for the Patriots, over half the global inventory has now been consumed in the Middle East. Similar to the THAAD interceptors as well."

— Kelly Grieco, missile expert, Stimson Center

CSIS warns that rebuilding those stockpiles could take three years or more, raising concerns about protecting US forces and bases worldwide if another major conflict erupts, particularly in the Pacific.

Competing Priorities

A US defense official told the Washington Post that Grynkewich's alert is consistent with past outreach from top generals when they identify risks requiring Washington's consideration. Commanders regularly compete for finite resources, the official said.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=jfbKS76YeHg

The strain has also affected Gulf state allies, which have drained many of their own antimissile interceptors. NBC News reported that US commanders have resorted to not shooting down Iranian projectiles on track to hit unpopulated areas of bases, seeking to conserve interceptor missiles.

The Pentagon's $67 billion emergency funding request for fiscal year 2026 includes $18.2 billion specifically to replace Patriot missiles, Navy Tomahawks, and THAAD interceptors. Half of the munitions requested in the 2027 budget are low-cost alternatives worth $600,000 or less.

Diplomatic Window

Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine told senators last week that without additional funding, the Pentagon will "not get the munitions" it needs. Caine also raised the dwindling stockpile directly with President Trump in a Friday meeting, where Trump was weighing a major escalation.

Trump subsequently signaled a pause in strikes, with diplomacy re-emerging as an option. "There's a military exit where we just keep going just the way we are, and we can even make it a heavier dose," Trump told reporters. "Or there's a smarter strategy that you make a deal. And they want to make a deal."

Gulf nations including Oman and Qatar are attempting to revive diplomatic channels with Tehran. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to meet Trump in Washington next week to discuss the situation.
nri_angle: The US military strain has broader implications for regional stability, affecting Indian diaspora members in the Middle East and Gulf states.
